summary:
MWAY is an interactive platform designed to make future human exploration of Mars safer, more efficient, and better organized.
We developed a 3D Mars mapping and mission-planning system that integrates scientific data from multiple NASA missions. The platform combines satellite imagery, topographic models, thermal observations, and geological information to support exploration planning.
MWAY uses the A* pathfinding algorithm to generate and compare routes based on distance, elevation, terrain slopes, and travel time. We also developed an interactive astronaut simulation that visualizes crew members directly on the Martian surface, allowing users to explore planned routes and simulate astronaut movements during missions.
The platform also supports crew management, scientific task scheduling, EVA planning, and resource calculations for oxygen, water, food, and electricity. Additional modules provide atmospheric and space-weather information.
MWAY addresses NASA's challenge by transforming scientific data into practical planning tools. Given Mars' extreme environment, limited resources, and communication delays with Earth, such tools are essential for supporting autonomous decisions and future human exploration.
details:
What Exactly Does It Do?

As human missions to Mars become possible in the future, engineers and mission planners will face many challenges. They will need to find safe routes across unfamiliar terrain, prepare for extreme environmental conditions, manage limited resources, and organize scientific activities far from Earth.
We developed MWAY as a prototype of a tool that could one day help engineers and mission planners prepare for these expeditions.
Our goal was to bring different aspects of mission planning together in one application. Instead of using separate tools to study the Martian surface, calculate routes, and organize missions, we wanted to create a platform where all these activities could be connected.

MWAY combines an interactive 3D map of Mars with scientific data from NASA, route-planning algorithms, crew management, resource calculations, and astronaut simulations.
The application allows users to explore the Martian surface, choose scientific destinations, plan expeditions, and visualize how astronauts might move across the terrain.

How Does It Work?

GitHub: https://github.com/nimbs-hack/mway

We developed several features that work together to make the planning process more interactive and practical.

Interactive 3D Mars Map

We started by creating a 3D map of Mars using real data from NASA missions. It combines satellite imagery, elevation models, thermal observations, and geological information.

Users can explore different areas of Mars, examine the terrain, switch between scientific layers, and select locations for research.

Intelligent Route Planning

We implemented the A pathfinding algorithm* to calculate routes across the Martian surface.

Instead of simply connecting two points with a straight line, the system considers distance, elevation changes, terrain slopes, and estimated travel time.

Users can compare different routing options, including faster routes, flatter paths, and alternative trajectories. We also added elevation profiles that help visualize changes in altitude and identify potentially difficult sections of a route.

Astronaut Simulation and HUD

One of the features we particularly enjoyed developing was the astronaut simulation.

We added astronauts directly to the 3D environment, allowing users to visualize their presence and simulate movement along planned routes.

We also developed an astronaut HUD and a helmet-view demonstration that display navigation information from a perspective inspired by what astronauts might see during a Marswalk.

This makes the experience more immersive and helps users better understand how an expedition could take place.

Crew and Mission Planning

We also created tools for organizing the mission itself.

Users can form crews, create mission phases, choose scientific destinations, assign tasks to astronauts, and schedule extravehicular activities (EVAs).

The application can review planned activities and identify scheduling conflicts, helping users organize the expedition more effectively.

Resource Calculations

We developed a system that estimates the resources required for a mission, including oxygen, water, food, and electricity.

The calculations use published NASA human-spaceflight reference values and consider crew size, mission duration, EVA activity, recycling efficiency, and additional resource reserves.

This allows users to compare different mission scenarios and understand how planning decisions affect resource requirements.

Environmental Information

We also developed components that provide information about the Martian environment using NASA datasets.

These include atmospheric observations, geological information, and space-weather data. We considered how terrain conditions, radiation, and environmental uncertainty could influence future exploration.

Some of these components are still being integrated and improved.

What Benefits Does It Have?

The main advantage of MWAY is that it brings different parts of mission planning together in one place.

A user can start by exploring the Martian surface, choose a scientific destination, calculate a route, assign astronauts, estimate the resources needed, and visualize how the expedition might unfold.

We focused on several important benefits:

Safer route planning: MWAY helps identify potentially challenging terrain, steep slopes, and route limitations before an expedition.

More efficient exploration: Users can compare routes, organize scientific activities, and estimate the time required to complete them.

Better resource management: The platform helps estimate the oxygen, water, food, and energy needed for different mission scenarios.

Scientific accessibility: Real NASA datasets become easier to explore and understand through interactive visualization.

More immersive planning: Astronaut simulations and HUD demonstrations help users visualize how future Marswalks could take place.

We also paid attention to the limitations of the available data. Some NASA datasets have insufficient resolution to identify small obstacles, environmental observations may not be available for every location, and resource estimates depend on simplified assumptions.

MWAY is still a prototype, so it cannot guarantee astronaut safety. However, we believe that combining these tools can make preliminary mission planning more understandable, organized, and useful.

What Do You Hope to Achieve?

Our long-term goal is to develop MWAY into a more advanced mission-planning tool that could potentially support engineers, researchers, and mission planners as human exploration of Mars becomes a reality.

We hope to improve the accuracy of route calculations, expand the available scientific data, and develop more detailed assessments of environmental risks and mission safety.

In the future, we would also like to integrate communication coverage analysis, emergency return planning, and more advanced simulations of astronaut activities.

Beyond its potential engineering applications, we believe MWAY could also be useful for education and scientific outreach. It gives students, researchers, and people interested in space exploration an opportunity to work with real NASA data and better understand the challenges of exploring another planet.

What makes MWAY important to us is that it connects scientific information with practical decisions.

We wanted to create something more than a visualization of Mars. Our goal was to build a platform where users could take real scientific data and use it to explore possible mission scenarios.

We know that the first human expeditions to Mars are still ahead of us, and there is much more work to be done before tools like MWAY could support real missions.

We hope our project can become a small step toward making future Mars exploration more informed, efficient, and safe.

What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Did You Use?

To develop MWAY, we combined different programming languages, visualization technologies, scientific datasets, and development tools.

Programming Languages and Frameworks:

React, TypeScript, and JavaScript — for developing the user interface and interactive mission-planning tools.

Go — for backend services, mission calculations, and resource estimation.

Vite and Bun — for organizing, developing, and building the web application.

3D Visualization and Navigation:

CesiumJS and WebGL — for displaying the 3D Martian surface, scientific layers, routes, and astronaut simulations.

A Pathfinding Algorithm* — for calculating terrain-aware routes based on distance, elevation, and movement restrictions.

NASA Data and Scientific Resources:

We used publicly available data from several NASA missions and scientific instruments:

NASA Mars Trek — planetary mapping, terrain models, and scientific layers.

Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) — high-resolution satellite imagery.

Mars Odyssey (THEMIS) — infrared observations of the Martian surface.

Mars Global Surveyor (MOLA and TES) — topographic and surface-property data.

Curiosity and Perseverance — atmospheric observations and scientific information.

NASA DONKI — information about solar activity and space-weather events.

USGS planetary geological maps — geological information about different regions of Mars.

AI-Assisted Development

We also used OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude during the development process.

These tools helped us write and review code, identify errors, explore implementation approaches, and improve different parts of the application.

They were especially useful when working with complex technologies and connecting separate components into one system.

Our team remained responsible for the project's concept, feature selection, design, integration, testing, and final decisions.

Hardware and Accessibility

MWAY was developed as a browser-based application that can run on standard computers without specialized hardware.

We wanted the platform to be accessible not only to developers, but also to students, researchers, and anyone interested in exploring Mars.

________

For us, MWAY is an opportunity to explore how the scientific knowledge NASA has collected over decades could help prepare for the next stage of human space exploration.

We brought together mapping, navigation, mission planning, resource calculations, and astronaut visualization because we believe these parts of an expedition should work together.

With MWAY, we want to turn NASA's scientific data into a practical tool for planning the future of human exploration on Mars.
